evidence: realtime_service.dart:222-227: `if (_attempt >= _maxAttempts) { Diag.record(DiagArea.app, 'rt_join_dead', ...); return; }` — nothing further is scheduled, so recovery depends entirely on the socket reopening. And `Diag.record` is a documented no-op: diag.dart:121 "Retired. Nothing below records anything.", with diag.dart:203 `if (!_capture) return;` and `_capture = false` unless `resetForTest` flips it (diag.dart:184). The same dead sink swallows `rt_join_retry` (realtime_service.dart:233), `rt_remove_failed` (realtime_service.dart:184) and `rt_resubscribe` (realtime_service.dart:176). `ErrorReporter` — which does work, and has 102 lifetime inserts in `client_errors` — is never called from this file.
fix: Replace the `rt_join_dead` Diag.record with `ErrorReporter.report(StateError('rt_join_dead: $_topic'), StackTrace.current, kind: 'realtime')` so a dead channel produces a row you can query, and surface a subtle 'reconnecting' indicator in the app bar when any always-on subscription has been unjoined for more than ~30s. Consider not capping retries at all for the always-on channels — cap the rate, not the count.

title: A widget that throws during build paints a featureless light-grey rectangle in the release build
userImpact: On a dark app, a chunk of the screen becomes a blank grey block with no text, no icon and no way to recover. The user cannot tell whether the app crashed, the content is missing, or they broke something. The only route out is force-closing.
evidence: `grep -rn 'ErrorWidget.builder|runZonedGuarded' lib/` → zero hits, so Flutter's defaults apply. In Flutter 3.44.2 (verified in the local SDK), `ErrorWidget._defaultErrorWidgetBuilder` (packages/flutter/lib/src/widgets/framework.dart:5667-5679) builds its `message` inside an `assert(() { ... }())`, which is stripped in release — so `message` stays `''`. `RenderErrorBox` then paints only `backgroundColor` (rendering/error.dart:156 `context.canvas.drawRect(offset & size, Paint()..color = backgroundColor)`), and `_initBackgroundColor()` (rendering/error.dart:114-121) returns `const Color(0xF0C0C0C0)` — light grey — outside debug. main.dart:59-62 correctly reports the error to `ErrorReporter` and then calls `FlutterError.presentError(details)`, which routes to exactly that grey box.
fix: Set `ErrorWidget.builder` in main.dart beside the existing handlers to return a small branded panel on `MilesColors.night` reading something like "Something went wrong here" with a retry/back affordance, sized to its constraints so it degrades gracefully inside a list row as well as full-screen.

title: The request timeout covers only the response headers, not the body — a stalled body still hangs forever
userImpact: The exact failure TimeoutHttpClient was written to prevent still happens on a flaky connection: a screen spins indefinitely with no error and nothing to tap, because the server answered and then stopped sending.
evidence: timeout_http_client.dart:38-46: `return _inner.send(request).timeout(limit, onTimeout: () => throw http.ClientException(...))` — the deadline applies to the future that completes when the `StreamedResponse` (headers) is returned. In http 1.6.0, `BaseClient._sendUnstreamed` ends with `return Response.fromStream(await send(request));` (pub cache base_client.dart:68) — and `Response.fromStream` awaits `stream.toBytes()` with no deadline of its own. Every Supabase query, RPC, auth call and function invoke goes through that path (supabase_service.dart:20 `httpClient: TimeoutHttpClient(http.Client())`).
fix: Wrap the whole exchange, not just the handshake: override `send` to return a StreamedResponse whose stream is itself deadline-bounded (e.g. `response.stream.timeout(limit)`), or keep a total-elapsed budget and fail the request when it is exceeded. Keep the existing larger `uploadTimeout` split for `/storage/v1/`.
effort: 3 hours including a test that stalls mid-body.

title: Chat history stops dead at 300 messages with no way to load earlier, and is re-fetched in full on every open
userImpact: Message 301 and everything older is unreachable. No 'load earlier' control, no indication that anything was truncated — the conversation simply appears to begin two weeks ago. For an active couple that is a fortnight of history, and every competitor (WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, iMessage) scrolls back forever. Opening the chat also costs a full 300-row fetch every time.
evidence: chat_repository.dart:334-340: `.from('messages').select().eq('couple_id', coupleId).order('created_at', ascending: false).limit(300)`. `grep -n 'loadMore|_loadOlder|paginat' lib/features/chat/chat_screen.dart` returns no pagination path — `_scroll`'s only listener is `_onScroll` (chat_screen.dart:698-702), which does nothing but clear the new-message chip. No local cache exists, so the 300 rows come over the wire on every entry. Note the pattern is already solved elsewhere in the codebase: `SharedMediaRepository.page()` (shared_media_repository.dart:45-63) does proper keyset pagination on `seq` with a `beforeSeq` cursor and a `pageSize` of 30.
fix: Reuse the SharedMediaRepository keyset pattern for chat: `fetchPage(coupleId, {int? beforeSeq})` ordered by `seq desc limit 50`, triggered when `_scroll` nears the top of the reversed list (`messages_couple_seq_idx` already exists to serve it). Cut the initial page from 300 to ~50 and the chat opens faster too.

title: On the default sign-up path no key escrow is ever written; the one prompt that fixes it is dismissible and asked exactly once, forever
userImpact: Plainly: a user who taps "Not now" once loses their private vault, Memory Threads and Wish Jar entries permanently the day they reinstall, factory-reset, or move to a new phone. The only rescue is a live ceremony with a partner who still holds the key. If both partners reinstall, or if the user forgets their password and resets it after the key is already gone, it is unrecoverable by anyone including the developer. Nothing warns them at the moment they decline.
evidence: With email confirmation on, `SupabaseRepository.signUp` returns before escrow: supabase_repository.dart:129 `if (res.session == null) return;`, and `KeyEscrow.backup(password)` is the line after (supabase_repository.dart:133). The confirmation link then creates the session with no password in hand — sign_up_page.dart:154, "If this address is new here, a confirmation link is on its way. Open it and you are in." — so `signIn()` (supabase_repository.dart:136-211), the only path that escrows with a password available, never runs. The backstop is `EscrowPrompt.maybeShow` (app_shell.dart:190), which returns early on a one-shot flag: escrow_prompt.dart:30 `if (prefs.getBool(_askedKey) ?? false) return;` and escrow_prompt.dart:42 `await prefs.setBool(_askedKey, true);` on decline. Password reset cannot repair it: `updatePassword` only re-seals when a seed is present (supabase_repository.dart:320 `escrowWritten: hasSeed && await KeyEscrow.backup(newPassword)`), and after a reinstall there is none. Live: `key_escrow` and `partner_rewrap_requests` both currently hold 0 rows.
fix: Escrow on the path that actually happens. Either require a password re-entry once at the end of onboarding (framed as 'protect your memories' rather than an out-of-context credential prompt), or switch the encrypted areas to a user-chosen recovery passphrase captured during onboarding and escrowed then. At minimum: make the decline re-askable (re-prompt after N days or on first vault/memory write rather than never), and show a persistent 'your memories are not backed up' state in Settings so the risk is visible rather than a one-frame dialog the user swiped past months ago.

title: 58 fully-empty catch blocks swallow failures with no log, no report and no user signal
userImpact: When something goes wrong the app usually does nothing at all — no message, no retry, no trace. Support emails become unanswerable because the failure left no record anywhere, on the device or the server.
evidence: `grep -rn 'catch (_) {}' lib/ --include=*.dart | wc -l` → **58**, against 380 total catch sites (`grep -rno 'catch\s*(' lib/ | wc -l`). Concentrated in the paths that matter most: call_controller.dart (11 occurrences incl. :1096, :1219, :1262, :1522, :1664, :1667, :1810, :1817, :1845), chat_screen.dart (:213, :593, :598, :605, :962), session_provider.dart (:223, :260, :282, :325), partner_here_badge.dart (:63, :107, :133, :145), rapid_camera_screen.dart (8). Separately, several read paths swallow into an empty result rather than an error — chat_repository.dart:314 and :344 skip malformed rows with `catch (_) {}` inside the parse loop, so 'parsed 12 of 300' is indistinguishable from 'there were 12'.
fix: Not a mass rewrite — triage. Any catch on a path the user is actively waiting on gets a visible outcome; any catch on a background path gets at minimum an `ErrorReporter.report(e, s, kind: '<area>')` so it exists in `client_errors`. For the row-parse loops, count skips and report when `parsed < received`. Then add a repo-hygiene test (you already have that harness in test/unit/hygiene/) that fails the build on a new bare `catch (_) {}`.
effort: 2-3 days for the triage, half a day for the lint test.

title: On-device media cache is bounded by object count, not bytes, so it can grow to multiple gigabytes
userImpact: Miles quietly becomes one of the largest apps on the phone. Users on 64 GB devices notice, and the app offers no cache size display and no clear-cache button, so the only remedy they find is uninstalling — which, given the escrow finding above, is also how they lose their vault.
evidence: encrypted_media_cache.dart:41-47: `CacheManager(Config('milesCipherMedia', stalePeriod: Duration(days: 90), maxNrOfCacheObjects: 1500))` — flutter_cache_manager caps entries, not bytes. The buckets those entries come from allow large files: `select id, file_size_limit from storage.buckets` → couple_intimate 104,857,600 and personal_vault 104,857,600 (100 MB each), couple_media and couple_files 26,214,400 (25 MB). 1500 objects averaging even 2 MB is 3 GB, and this sits alongside `DefaultCacheManager`'s separate 200-object store used by CachedNetworkImage. Note the RAM layer got this right — `_l2MaxBytes = 48 * 1024 * 1024` (encrypted_media_cache.dart:57) with the comment "bounded by BYTES rather than by entry count... One byte ceiling self-balances and cannot be wrong" — the disk layer just never received the same treatment.
fix: Apply the same reasoning one layer down: track total bytes for the L1 store and evict LRU past a ceiling (1-2 GB is generous), or lower `maxNrOfCacheObjects` and exclude full-size originals from L1 so only tiles and covers persist. Add a Storage row in Settings showing cache size with a Clear button — it is also the honest answer to 'why is this app 3 GB'.

title: The first screen of onboarding replaces its own helpful validation messages with "Something went wrong. Please try again."
userImpact: Every new user is force-routed to /welcome. If they tap Continue without a name or without picking a date of birth, they get a generic failure that names no field and offers no next step. The app knows exactly what is wrong and refuses to say it. This is the very first thing a stranger does in your app.
evidence:
mobile/lib/features/auth/welcome_page.dart:80-92 throws StateError('Please tell us your name.') / StateError('Please enter your date of birth.'), then line 113 does `_error = friendlyAuthError(e)`. friendlyAuthError (mobile/lib/features/auth/auth_errors.dart:9-72) has no StateError branch, so it falls through to line 72's generic string.
Proved by running a probe test against the real function:
  IN : Please tell us your name.
  OUT: Something went wrong. Please try again.
  IN : Please enter your date of birth.
  OUT: Something went wrong. Please try again.
  IN : You must be 18 or older to use Miles.
  OUT: Something went wrong. Please try again.
(probe file deleted after the run; tree is clean)
The path is mandatory: mobile/lib/core/app/router.dart:111-113 redirects any account without an onboarded profile to /welcome.
fix: Two options. Cleanest: validate inline and never throw for field validation — set `_error` (or per-field errors) directly and return, keeping friendlyAuthError for the network/Supabase call only. Minimal: add `if (e is StateError) return e.message;` as the first line of friendlyAuthError — couple_page.dart:108 already uses exactly that idiom, so the codebase already knows the answer in one place and not the other.

title: The pairing screen prints raw exceptions, including your Supabase hostname and RPC name, straight to the user
userImpact: Screen two of onboarding. A user who taps Join with no signal sees a developer stack string naming your backend host and endpoint. It looks broken and unprofessional, tells them nothing actionable, and leaks your project ref to anyone who screenshots it. The identical failure elsewhere in the app produces a clean "Couldn't reach the server" message.
evidence:
mobile/lib/features/auth/couple_page.dart:108 — `_error = e is StateError ? e.message : e.toString();` rendered into an AlertBanner.
redeemPairingInvite (mobile/lib/core/data/supabase_repository.dart:535-559) maps five known Postgrest messages to friendly StateErrors and then `rethrow`s everything else — so network failures and unmapped Postgrest errors hit the raw `e.toString()` branch.
Probe output of exactly what line 108 renders:
  ClientException: Failed host lookup: 'sopictusdonlvuezmfep.supabase.co' (OS Error: No address associated with hostname, errno = 7), uri=https://sopictusdonlvuezmfep.supabase.co/rest/v1/rpc/redeem_pairing_invite
  PostgrestException(message: new row violates row-level security policy for table "couple_members", code: 42501, details: Forbidden, hint: null)
Contrast: _create() on the same screen (line 87) already uses friendlyAuthError(e) — two different error policies on one screen.
fix: Change line 108 to `e is StateError ? e.message : friendlyAuthError(e)`. That preserves the five good pairing messages and routes everything else through the offline/rate-limit copy that already exists. Then add the StateError branch from the finding above so the two lines collapse into one call.

title: The GIF picker tells end users to go register a developer account at giphy.com
userImpact: A user opens the GIF button in chat while offline (or during any edge-function hiccup) and is told: register at developers.giphy.com, create an app, and add a key to the app. They cannot do any of that. It is the single most developer-facing string in the product and it reads as an unfinished app.
evidence:
mobile/lib/features/chat/widgets/giphy_picker.dart:123-124:
  'GIFs need a free GIPHY key.\n\nGet one at developers.giphy.com → '
  'Create App, then add it to the app as GIPHY_API_KEY.'
Shown whenever `GiphyService.isConfigured` is false (line 118). The key is fetched at runtime from the `giphy-key` edge function (mobile/lib/core/services/giphy_service.dart:60) inside a try/catch that only debugPrints on failure (line 67), so any network failure lands here.
The key IS present in prod, so this is the failure path, not the normal one — live query on app_secrets returned GIPHY_API_KEY: set (len 32). Offline is a common state, so this string is reachable by ordinary users.
fix: Replace with user-language copy and a retry, matching the rest of the app: "GIFs aren't loading right now. Check your connection and try again." plus a Try again button that re-invokes the key fetch. The developer instructions belong in the README, not in the chat sheet.

title: No text-scaling support anywhere in 238 files — large-font users are an untested population
userImpact: Android font size goes to 200% and is one of the most-used accessibility settings. Nothing in the app clamps or adapts to it, and the layout leans on hundreds of fixed pixel values. Users on large fonts are likely to hit clipped text and overflow stripes on some screens. Reviews from that group are brutal and specific.
evidence:
grep for textScaler / textScaleFactor / TextScaler across mobile/lib -> 0 hits.
grep -c 'fontSize:' across mobile/lib -> 457.
grep -c 'height: <2+ digits>' across mobile/lib -> 411.
Only 30 uses of maxLines and 24 of TextOverflow.ellipsis across the whole app.
The team clearly knows the risk in places — mobile/lib/features/home/home_screen.dart:187-189 comments "the mark at a large text scale would otherwise overflow the row outright" and wraps in Flexible — but it is handled case by case, not systematically.
UNVERIFIED: I did not run the app, so I cannot name which screens actually overflow. What is verified is that nothing guards against it.
fix: Two passes. (1) Ship a global clamp in main.dart's MaterialApp builder — wrap with MediaQuery.withClampedTextScaling(maxScaleFactor: 1.3 or 1.5) — one line that bounds the blast radius immediately. (2) Then run the app at 200% font and walk Home, Chat, Settings, Closer, Cycle and fix what actually breaks. Do not skip (2); the clamp buys time, it is not the fix.
effort: 1 line for the clamp, half a day for the walkthrough

title: Twelve different date formats, mixing day-first and month-first, none of them locale-aware
userImpact: The same app shows "12 Aug" on one screen and "Aug 12, 2026" on another. A user in the UK or Pakistan sees US-ordered dates on half the screens and their own ordering on the other half. It is the kind of thing nobody reports but everybody feels as sloppiness.
evidence:
Inventory of DateFormat patterns across mobile/lib:
  day-first:   'd MMM y'  chat/widgets/media_viewer.dart:791
               'd MMM'    profile/partner_profile_screen.dart:464, rituals/rituals_screen.dart:396 and :403
  month-first: 'MMM d, y' timeline/timeline_screen.dart:306 and :514
               'MMM d, y · h:mm a' vault/vault_screen.dart:412
               'MMMM d, y' capsule/capsule_detail_screen.dart:327
               'MMMM d'   capsule/capsule_detail_screen.dart:357
               'MMM d'    capsule/capsule_detail_screen.dart:369
               'MMM d, h:mm a' auth/couple_page.dart:379
All are hardcoded pattern strings, so none respond to device locale. Capsule alone uses three different formats on one screen.
fix: Add a small mobile/lib/core/time/date_format.dart with three named helpers (shortDate, longDate, dateTime) built from DateFormat.yMMMd(locale) / .jm(locale), and replace all twelve call sites. Locale-aware constructors also fix the day-first/month-first split for free.

title: The launch guard you documented as test-enforced does not exist, and a stale comment claims a live URL is missing
userImpact: No direct user impact — but you believe a safety net is protecting your launch and it is not. Doc comments in this repo are unusually load-bearing (they are how sessions hand off), so a false one is more expensive here than in most codebases.
evidence:
mobile/lib/features/legal/terms_text.dart:39-40 defines `milesTermsHasContact`, and its doc comment at line 36-38 says "a release must not ship without them, and a test asserts that rather than trusting anyone to remember." grep for milesTermsHasContact across mobile/lib and mobile/test returns only the declaration itself and the comment referencing it — no caller, no test.
Separately, mobile/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart:1010-1011 still says "The policy is written ... and not yet hosted, so [milesPrivacyPolicyUrl] is empty." It is no longer empty (terms_text.dart:23 points at the live Vercel URL, which returns 200). The comment is stale and would mislead the next session.
fix: Either write the test the comment promises (assert milesTermsHasContact is true, in the same hygiene suite as the launcher-disguise test) or delete the getter and its comment. Update the settings_screen.dart:1010 comment to match reality.

title: Signups accept known-breached passwords
userImpact: A stranger can create an account on your couples app with a password that is already in public breach corpora. Given what this app holds — private photos, a vault, location — account takeover via credential stuffing is the realistic threat, and it is one toggle away from being mitigated.
evidence: Supabase security advisor on prod sopictusdonlvuezmfep returned lint `auth_leaked_password_protection` at level WARN: "Leaked password protection is currently disabled." The app's own minimum is only 8 characters (mobile/lib/features/auth/sign_up_page.dart:55 — 'Use at least 8 characters.'), with no other strength requirement.
fix: Enable leaked-password protection in the Supabase dashboard (Authentication → Policies). It checks against HaveIBeenPwned at signup and costs nothing. The existing friendlyAuthError already has a `weak_password` branch (auth_errors.dart:26-28), so the rejection message is already written.

title: A new chat message produces no notification at all — the notify branch that would draw one is dead code
userImpact: Partner sends a message. The other phone shows nothing: no banner, no sound, no badge. They find out next time they happen to open the app. For an app whose primary surface is chat, this is the single fastest route to a 1-star review and an uninstall. Two users who talk constantly never noticed; strangers will notice on day one.
evidence: Live prod trigger `notify_message()` (pg_get_functiondef, sopictusdonlvuezmfep) posts `'kind','msg_sync'` only. Client handler mobile/lib/core/services/reach_notifications.dart:412-423 — `if (type == 'msg_sync')` … comment: "it draws NOTHING. No channel, no notification, no sound, no badge — the recipient is never told anything arrived." The branch that WOULD notify, reach_notifications.dart:425-439 (`type == 'message'` → showMessageNotification), is never reached because nothing ever sends kind 'message'. Foreground path mobile/lib/core/services/fcm_service.dart:266,284 also draws nothing. supabase/functions/reach-notify/index.ts:36 states the reason outright: "The owner does not want message notifications."
fix: Add a `notify_message` path that sends kind 'message' with a generic title (the cover identity's name, no sender, no preview — disguise_notification.dart already builds neutral copy), plus a Settings toggle for people who genuinely want silence. Keep msg_sync for the delivery ack. This is a deliberate 2-user decision that does not survive contact with strangers — say so in the release notes if it ships off by default.

title: Private Vault media cannot be saved OR read unless the user first opens Closer — which is hidden by default
userImpact: Brand new couple. They open the drawer → Vault → set a PIN → Add → pick photos. Every single one fails, and the app says "Nothing could be saved — check your connection." Their connection is fine. Existing vault thumbnails also fail to decrypt on every cold start. The one feature the whole app's privacy promise hangs on is unusable for anyone who has not first wandered into a module that ships switched off.
evidence:
PROVEN, not inferred. Probe run in mobile/: `flutter test` on a one-line call to CryptoCore.encryptBytes with no derived key →
  `AUDIT: encryptBytes THREW -> StateError: Bad state: no shared key — refusing to write unencrypted content`
Chain: vault_screen.dart:191 → vault_repository.dart:213 `CryptoCore.encryptBytesOffThread(...)` → crypto_core.dart:576-586 throws when `_sharedKey == null && !_plaintextAgreed`. `_sharedKey` is assigned non-null in exactly one place, crypto_core.dart:393 inside `deriveSharedKey`, whose only callers are closer_crypto.dart:47, wish_jar_repository.dart, partner_rewrap.dart:405 — none on the vault or app-boot path (`grep -rn "deriveSharedKey|ensureSharedKey(" lib/core lib/main.dart lib/features/vault` returns nothing for vault/boot). Read side fails identically: crypto_core.dart:734 `throw StateError('encrypted media but no couple key')`. And Closer is hidden by default — live prod: `couples.modest_mode` column_default = `true`. The failure is then reported as a network error at vault_screen.dart:209.
fix: Call `ensureSharedKey(session)` (or a vault-specific equivalent) in VaultGateScreen before the vault opens, and surface its real StateError text instead of the connection toast. Longer term the personal vault should not be sealed under the *couple* key at all — see the unpair finding.
effort: 2-4 hours for the gate; 1-2 days to re-key the vault properly

title: Leaving your partner permanently destroys your own Private Vault, and the confirmation dialog promises the opposite
userImpact: This is the exact scenario the app is supposed to protect. Someone in a bad relationship taps Settings → Partner → Remove partner. The dialog reassures them: "Your private data and time capsules are preserved." Every photo, video and file in their personal vault becomes permanently undecryptable the moment the couple ends, because the key was never theirs. They lose the private material they collected, having been told in writing it was safe.
evidence: Vault media is sealed with the COUPLE shared key: vault_repository.dart:213,222 call `CryptoCore.encryptBytesOffThread`, which uses `_sharedKey` derived by ECDH against the partner's published X25519 key (crypto_core.dart:389-396). After `leave_couple()` (live prod definition: nulls `profiles.couple_id` for both) `session.partner` is null, so `ensureSharedKey` throws at closer_crypto.dart:23 and no derivation path exists. Decrypt then throws unconditionally: crypto_core.dart:661-664 and :734. The key ring cannot help — crypto_core.dart:632 loads it only when a current key already exists. Dialog text: mobile/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart:334-336.
fix: Seal personal_vault under a per-user key derived from the user's own X25519 seed (already escrowed, already reinstall-survivable) with its own HKDF label — never the couple key. Migrate existing rows on read. Until that lands, the Remove-partner dialog must not say private data is preserved.

title: The vault note composer promises "only you can ever read this" for text the app stores in plaintext
userImpact: A user types their most private thought into a box that says nobody else can ever read it. It lands in Postgres as readable text. Anyone with database access — the owner, Supabase support, anyone who gets a backup — can read it. The app's own FAQ, in the same binary, admits this. That is a false security representation, and it is the kind of thing that ends up in a screenshot on social media.
evidence: mobile/lib/features/vault/vault_screen.dart:256 hintText: 'Just for you — only you can ever read this'; :494 'Add a private note only you can see.' Write path vault_repository.dart:126-134 inserts `'content': content` with no encryption call. Live prod schema: `personal_vault_items.content` is `text` (information_schema query). The app's own FAQ contradicts it — faq_text.dart:67-71: "a plain text note typed into the Private Vault is stored unencrypted. Only the vault's files are sealed."
fix: Either encrypt note bodies the same way the files are, or change both strings to match the FAQ ("Only you can open this in the app" / add a one-line 'notes are not end-to-end encrypted' caption). Do not leave the two texts disagreeing inside one build.

title: "Delete account" claims to delete your messages and photos; with a partner still paired it deletes neither
userImpact: Someone wants out. They type DELETE and read "This permanently deletes your account, your messages, your photos and videos." Their account goes. Every message they ever sent, every photo and video, stays fully readable in their ex-partner's app forever. They walk away believing it is gone. This is both a trust failure and a thin position under a GDPR erasure request.
evidence: Dialog: mobile/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart:426-429. Live prod `delete_my_account()` (pg_get_functiondef): `delete from public.messages where couple_id = v_couple;` and the storage_reap inserts are BOTH inside `if v_others = 0`. With a partner remaining it only sets `profiles.couple_id = null` for the caller, reaps `personal_vault` objects, and deletes the auth user. Shared messages, gallery_items, memory_threads and couple storage are untouched. (The FAQ at faq_text.dart:239-245 states this correctly — only the dialog is wrong.)
fix: Rewrite the dialog to match the FAQ wording, and offer an explicit second choice: "also delete the conversation from your partner's copy" (a couple-scoped purge the remaining partner is told about). Do not ship a delete button that overstates what it does.
effort: 3 hours for the copy; 1 day for the shared-history purge option

title: No off switch for online status, typing, read receipts, or which screen you are on
userImpact: Your partner sees a live feed of you: online/last-seen, "typing…", green read ticks, and "In Chat" / "In Gallery" — which feature of the app you are currently looking at. There is no way to turn any of it off. WhatsApp, Signal, Instagram and Telegram all ship read-receipt and last-seen controls precisely because a couples context is where they get weaponised. As shipped, a controlling partner gets a minute-by-minute activity monitor and the other person has no setting to reach for.
evidence: Full inventory of mobile/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart section headers (lines 522, 574, 591, 629, 645, 669, 685, 710, 727, 773, 818, 840): Profile, Timezone, Language, Disguise, Location sharing, Reach alerts, Privacy (Closer visibility only), Security (biometric lock), Partner, Safety, Account, About. Nothing for presence. `grep -rniE "read receipt|typing_enabled|share_presence|invisible|appear offline|hide_online"` across lib/ returns only comments, no setting. Broadcast writes are unconditional: presence_service.dart:404 `setScreen`, :353 `setTyping`, :369 `setChatLastRead`, and presence_route_observer.dart:204 pushes the screen name on every route change. Home renders it at home_screen.dart:414-418 ("In ${presence.currentScreen}").
fix: One Privacy section with four switches — Online status, Typing indicator, Read receipts, Activity (current screen) — gated at the four `_upsert` call sites in presence_service.dart. Make read receipts symmetric (off means you stop seeing theirs), the way every competitor does it. Default Activity to OFF; it is the most surveillance-shaped of the four and no competitor ships anything like it.

title: No way to recover a forgotten vault PIN — the content is simply gone
userImpact: Four digits, set once, protecting everything a person considered too private for the shared app. Forget it and there is no "Forgot PIN?" link anywhere — no reset, no email path, no escrow question. The only route is emailing the owner's personal Gmail, and he cannot help either. Guaranteed support mail, and an angry one.
evidence: `grep -rn "forgot|Forgot|reset.*pin|recover" mobile/lib/features/vault/` → no matches. vault_gate_screen.dart:283-285 offers only PIN entry and biometric; the only other affordance is a back arrow (:290). Verification and lockout are server-side bcrypt (vault_repository.dart:94-101, `verify_vault_pin` returning 'ok'|'wrong'|'locked'|'no_pin'), so nothing on-device can bypass it. This is also still open on the project's own task list (#6 "Honest failures + PIN recovery", pending).
fix: Add "Forgot PIN" → re-authenticate with the account password (or the escrow password, which already exists) → `set_vault_pin` with a new one. The PIN is an access gate, not the encryption key, so a password-backed reset loses nothing.

title: The panic gesture advertised in the FAQ does nothing on a default install
userImpact: The FAQ tells a frightened user there is a panic gesture: shake three times, or volume-up plus volume-down, and the app drops back to its cover screen. On the default install — which is now every install, both channels — no cover is set, so the gesture produces a single frame of flicker and the real app is right back on screen. Someone testing it decides the safety feature is broken; someone relying on it in the moment gets nothing.
evidence: Claim: mobile/lib/features/legal/faq_text.dart:108-112. Both flavors now ship `PLAIN_DEFAULT = true` (android/app/build.gradle.kts:107 sideload, :155 play), so the stored identity is `kPlainProfile` with `cover: DisguiseCover.none`. `_emergencyLock()` (main.dart:244-247) calls only `MilesApp.raiseCover()` → `showRealApp = false` (main.dart:160-162) → DisguiseCoverHost sees `d.cover == DisguiseCover.none` and immediately calls `widget.onAuthenticated()` (disguise_cover_host.dart:56-58), reopening the app. `_emergencyLock` never calls `AppLock.lock()`.
fix: Make the panic gesture call `AppLock.lock()` (the LockScreen overlay already exists and is wired at main.dart:223) whenever no cover is set, so it locks instead of no-opping. Then the FAQ sentence becomes true for both configurations.

title: "Only your partner can ever see this" under Location sharing is not true of the server
userImpact: A user deciding whether to share precise GPS reads a flat guarantee that only their partner can ever see it. Coordinates are stored as plain numbers the operator can read. Every other privacy string in this app is scrupulously hedged; this one is not, and location is the field people are most careful about.
evidence: mobile/lib/features/settings/settings_screen.dart:651. Live prod schema: `presence.latitude` / `presence.longitude` are `double precision`, `location_label` is `text` — no ciphertext columns. Live read of the table returns readable values, e.g. location_label 'Al Haram, Al Madinah Province, Saudi Arabia' with lat/lon populated. The FAQ is correctly hedged for the same data ("chat, media, location, profile … not end-to-end encrypted", faq_text.dart:71-73); only this subtitle overstates.
fix: Change to "Only your partner sees this in the app" or "Shared with your partner only". One string.

title: Unpairing orphans a presence row carrying your last known coordinates, outside every retention job
userImpact: The FAQ promises the couple's entire history is deleted 30 days after a breakup. The row holding your last precise GPS fix is not part of that promise in practice — it survives indefinitely, and the only thing that ever removes it is deleting your account. For someone who left a relationship because of where they now live, that is the exact record they wanted gone.
evidence: `leaveCouple()` (supabase_repository.dart:589-595) updates only couple_id/is_online/app_last_active_at — latitude, longitude, location_label and location_sharing_mode are left set. Once `couple_id` is null, `prune_dissolved_couples()` (live definition) cannot reach the row: it deletes couples, and presence cascades via `presence_couple_id_fkey`, which no longer matches. No cron job targets presence directly (`select * from cron.job` — 10 jobs, none touch presence). Live prod already holds one orphaned row: user 8202e6da-…, couple_id null. Compounding it, the comment at supabase_repository.dart:584 claims "The SQL function clears presence server-side" — the live `leave_couple()` body never mentions presence, and the client cleanup that actually does it sits inside a swallow-all `catch (_)` at :596.
fix: Clear the location columns inside `leave_couple()` itself (server-side, where it cannot be skipped by a dropped connection), and delete the correspondingly stale comment. Add a prune for presence rows with a null couple_id older than 30 days.

title: Menstrual cycle data is shared with the partner by default
userImpact: A woman logs a period. Her partner can already see it — she was never asked. Special-category health data defaulting to shared, in an app whose whole pitch is that the user controls what is visible, is the wrong way round; Flo, Clue and Natural Cycles all make partner sharing an explicit opt-in.
evidence: mobile/lib/features/cycle/cycle_repository.dart:11 `this.shareWithPartner = true` and :20 `(j['share_with_partner'] as bool?) ?? true`. The toggle exists (cycle_screen.dart:271-279) but is on before anyone touches it. The partner-facing surface is already built (partner_cycle_card.dart), so the first log is visible immediately.
fix: Flip the default to false and ask once, on the first log: "Share this with <name>?" with a clear off option. One line plus a prompt.
